papers.what_it_is: A neural-network method that learns an effective quantum channel (a Stinespring-dilation ansatz with a learned unitary) from discrete-time dynamics, tested on simulated Lindblad and circuit data and on cross-talk on the 27-qubit ibmq ehningen processor.

existing.note: The 27-qubit statement is on PDF p.5 and the shot count on p.6 (the stored anchor says p.8). The paper also gives the access date, 3rd of January 2024 (Appendix B 2, p.8).
existing.value: The authors state that the device experiment used the 27-qubit ibmq ehningen processor with 20 000 shots in each of 9 Pauli bases.
quotes: In the following, we explore quantum channels that are implemented on the 27-qubit ibmq ehningen NISQ processor.
We run a total of 20 000 shots in each of the 9 necessary Pauli bases.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Sec. III C.

existing.note: The passage is on PDF p.3 (the stored anchor says p.5). The same section adds that the method can in principle be adapted to non-Markovian dynamics by learning a family of channels from the initial time to each later time; that is a proposal, not a tested result.

quotes: On the one hand, while we can train the network using any dynamics, this assumption clearly represents a limitation on its ability to capture generic evolutions.
Before we proceed, we comment on our underlying assumption of Markovianity
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in Sec. II C.

existing.value: The authors report that, for a circuit of repeated native gates on two neighbouring qubits (qubit 4 and qubit 7) with the other qubits idle, the learned channel captures weak, yet evident, cross-talk effects, shown by a nonzero Pearson correlation coefficient.

on two neighboring qubits (namely qubit 4 and qubit 7), while leaving the remaining ones idle.

assertions.value: The authors state that they model the channel by the Stinespring dilation, with a unitary U acting on the system and an auxiliary particle, and that they parametrize U with a neural network whose output is constrained to be a unitary matrix.
quotes: We parametrize U through a neural-network and constrain the
to be a unitary matrix by means of Pytorch’s torch.nn.utils.parametrizations.orthogonal

assertions.value: The authors state that constraining the output of the network to be unitary ensures that the model represents a physical, that is completely positive and trace preserving, quantum channel.
quotes: This last step is necessary to ensure that our model
allows us to encode physical constraints directly into the neural-network ansatz
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement by the authors about their own construction, not tested separately.

assertions.value: The paper cites the result that any physical open-system dynamics can be represented with at most d squared Kraus operators, where d is the Hilbert-space dimension, and that the minimal number needed for a given channel is its Kraus rank.
quotes: any possible physical (open-system) dynamics can be represented by considering, at most, dE = d2 Kraus operators [17, 55].
The minimal dE required to represent a given quantum channel is the so-called Kraus rank [55].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that they minimize a loss proportional to the average square distance between the exact and the predicted density matrices with the Adam optimizer, and validate the learned channel on r = 10 additional initial conditions.
quotes: To perform the minimization we utilize the Adam optimizer [82].
After the training, we validate the learned channel against data generated from r = 10 additional initial conditions
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own training and validation setup in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state that the environmental dimension is treated as a hyper-parameter and that they explore values different from the Kraus rank required by the exact dynamics.
quotes: the environmental dimension dE can also be considered as a hyper-parameter of the model.
we explore values of dE different from the Kraus rank required by the exact dynamics
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors propose, without testing it in the paper, that the method can be adapted to non-Markovian discrete-time dynamics by learning the different channels that map the system from the initial time to each later time.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II C, p.3; Abstract, p.1
quotes: Instead of learning a single channel E implementing single-time updates, one could learn the different quantum channels mapping the system from the initial time to each later time t.
While the present approach is tailored for learning Markovian dynamics, we discuss how it can be adapted to also capture generic non-Markovian discrete-time evolutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposal by the authors, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for the single-qubit time-periodic Lindblad benchmark, the dynamics is accurately inferred for sufficiently large training sets and auxiliary dimension dE of at least 3.

assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result on one simulated benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the parameters (Ex/Ez, ω/Ez) = (0.5, 1) a Floquet generator exists in principle, yet the Lindblad approximator of Ref. [79] cannot discover it, while the learned channel reproduces the dynamics.

assertions.value: The authors report that inferring the channel directly gives a very high accuracy throughout the whole explored parameter regime, with the error below 10−4, including the region where no time-independent Lindblad description exists; the channels were learned with dE = 4 and M = 30 trajectories.
quotes: [see blue region indicating ϵ < 10−4 in Fig. 3(b)].
Error measure associated with the learned channels with dE = 4 that were trained on M = 30 different trajectories.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reduced-subsystem task is to learn the dynamics of two adjacent qubits in a circuit of L qubits, that the network is trained for times t = 1, ...10 and validated up to T = 20, and that for generic circuit parameters the dynamics is not expected to be Markovian.
quotes: We train the network for times t = 1, ...10 and validate the learned dynamics up to T = 20.
For generic values of the parameters φx and φnn, such dynamics is not expected to be Markovian.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Sec. III B.

assertions.value: The authors report that for (φx, φnn) = (0.5, 1) the dynamics is not accurately captured by the Markovian approximation, even at short times, while for (0.1, 0.1) the discrepancy arises mainly at later times.
quotes: We consider three parameter regimes: (φx, φnn) = (0.1, 0.1), (φx, φnn) = (0.5, 1)
the dynamics in the second case [cf. Fig. 4(b)] is not accurately captured by the Markovian approximation, even at short times.
for the first parameter pair, a discrepancy between the learned and the exact dynamics primarily arises at later times [cf. Fig. 4(a)].

assertions.value: The authors report that for an even larger coupling the approximation through the inferred Markovian model can improve again, and they suggest this may be due to faster mixing in the unitary circuit.
quotes: we observed that for even larger values of φnn [cf. Fig. 4(c)], the approximation through the inferred Markovian model can improve again, which may be due to faster mixing effects in the unitary circuit dynamics.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result with an untested explanation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hardware data were taken on the ibmq ehningen processor accessed on the 3rd of January 2024, with measurements for t = 11 to 20, and were split into M = 30 initial conditions for training and r = 10 for validation.

quotes: (accessed on the 3rd of January 2024)
and by performing measurements for t = 11, 12 . . . 20.

we pre-train the algorithm by estimating the state at t = 10 and learning in the time window t = 11, 12, . . . 20.

assertions.value: The authors report that the validation error shows it is possible to learn a quantum channel that accurately reproduces the circuit dynamics on the ibmq ehningen, even with relatively small data sets.
quotes: demonstrates that it is possible to learn a quantum channel that accurately reproduces the circuit dynamics on the ibmq ehningen.
This is possible even with relatively small data sets

assertions.value: The authors report that the learned channel approximates the actual device dynamics better than the ideal gate does, although the error for the ideal gate is quite small, and that the error does not rise for the last 10 trajectories, which were not used for training.
quotes: Despite the error for the ideal X gate being quite small for all the considered initial conditions, our algorithm can better approximate the actual dynamics.
Despite this, the error measure does not show an increase for the last 10 trajectories, indicating a good extrapolation capability of the model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device.

assertions.value: The authors state that they extract the ZZ-coupling strength V by fitting the Pearson correlation coefficients with the gate model of Eq. (6), and choose V in the range from −0.003 to −0.001 for the comparison.
quotes: we provide the ZZ-coupling strength V that we extract by fitting the Pearson correlation coefficients using the Hamiltonian in Eq. (6).
Based on this observation, we choose V ∈ (−0.003, −0.001) for the comparison in the main text.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical fit from one device.

assertions.value: The authors state that the large purity of the quantum state observed on the device is reflected in the network's ability to learn the dynamics with a relatively small environmental dimension.
quotes: the ability of the network to learn the dynamics with relatively small dE.
assertions.certainty_reason: An interpretation by the authors, not tested separately.

assertions.value: The paper attributes to cited work that cross-talk between neighbouring qubits on superconducting devices leads to a spurious ZZ-coupling that generates correlations between otherwise uncoupled qubits.
quotes: it has been observed that cross-talk effects between neighboring qubits lead to the emergence of a spurious ZZ-coupling [93–97]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report that for a single-qubit channel related to transposition, which the paper cites as not describable by any Lindblad master equation, the learned channel is very accurate as soon as dE is at least 3, the Kraus rank of the exact dynamics, and more accurate than the Lindblad approximator.
quotes: this quantum channel cannot be described by any (time-dependent) Lindblad master equation.
the learned channel is very accurate as soon as dE ≥ 3, which coincides with the Kraus rank of the exact dynamics [26]

assertions.value: The authors report that for an interacting open two-qubit system with time-independent Lindblad dynamics the method infers the dynamics with arbitrary precision given sufficiently large dE and M, and they conclude that the larger errors in other two-qubit examples come from non-Markovian effects rather than a deficiency of the model.
quotes: our method infers the dynamics with arbitrary precision, given sufficiently large dE and M
originates from non-Markovian effects rather than a possible deficiency of our model to infer dynamics of systems consisting of more than one qubit.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the strong-coupling case the circuit quickly drives the system toward the fully mixed state, which the learned channel mimics accurately, but small deviations from the mixed state are not fully captured.
quotes: This behavior may be attributed to a faster scrambling in the circuit which quickly drives the system toward the fully mixed state.
However, small deviations from this mixed state are not fully captured by the learned quantum channel.

quotes: proposed methods either rely on an ad-hoc ansatz, require data which are not experimentally accessible, or lack physical interpretability
assertions.certainty_reason: A characterization of other work by the authors, without a comparison in the paper.

quotes: The latter is based on a collision-model representation of quantum channels, which guarantees its physical consistency.
it would be interesting to explore how our neural-network method performs when training solely from partial information of the density matrix

papers.what_it_is: A Phasecraft paper that uses noisy QAOA samples as warm starts for classical heuristics (tabu search) on Max-Cut and Maximum Independent Set, with parameter-setting, routing and error-mitigation methods, measured in emulation and on IBM hardware by a Q-factor speedup ratio.

existing.note: The statement is on PDF p.31 (Section IX). The paper's next sentences name the open questions: problem size, benchmarking against best-in-class classical solvers, and the full-pipeline runtime.
existing.value: The authors state that several questions remain to be answered before the approach can be said to have delivered a genuine quantum advantage.
quotes: Despite this, several questions remain to be answered before this approach can be said to have delivered a genuine quantum advantage.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in Section IX.

existing.note: The paper states the values exceeding 1000 as reached 'in certain cases'. The Q-factor is a ratio of classical-heuristic iteration counts against random-start tabu search; the paper states that the runtime comparison does not include the time to generate the warm starts. The largest Q-factors reported for hardware in the results sections are about 600 (random graphs, N = 30) and a several-thousand-fold speedup for the line-graph frequency filter, a problem a greedy method solves easily.
existing.value: The authors report that quantum warm starts significantly improve classical heuristics such as tabu search where those rely on random initializations, with a Q-factor speedup exceeding 1000 in certain cases; they state that the runtime comparison does not include the time taken to generate the warm starts or random samples, so it is not a fair final comparison.

quotes: The speedup, as measured by the Q-factor, reaches values exceeding 1000× in certain cases, with performance gains persisting across different problem sizes.

the introduction of quantum warm starts significantly improves the performance of classical heuristics like tabu search in instances where classical optimization algorithms rely on random initializations.
this runtime comparison does not include the time taken to generate the warm starts or random samples in either case, meaning it is not a fair final comparison.

assertions.value: The authors describe quantum-enhanced optimization: noisy samples from a near-term quantum algorithm such as QAOA are used as a warm start to accelerate classical optimization algorithms, which then find a good solution more quickly than without the warm start.
quotes: noisy samples from a near-term quantum algorithm such as QAOA are used as a “warm start” to accelerate classical optimization algorithms.
The classical heuristic finds a good solution to the overall problem, ideally an optimal one, more quickly than it would have done without the warm start.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that removing the variational optimization part of QAOA means the quantum computer only needs to be accessed once, at the start of the algorithm, and that they introduce methods for choosing QAOA parameters for Max-Cut, Maximum Independent Set and general QUBO problems without variational optimization.
quotes: If the variational optimization part of QAOA is removed, the quantum computer only needs to be accessed once, at the start of the algorithm.
Here we introduce new methods for choosing good QAOA parameters for Max-Cut and Maximum Independent Set (MIS)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum-enhanced algorithm should degrade gracefully with noise, because under completely catastrophic depolarizing noise the quantum output is a uniformly random bit-string, which is what the classical algorithm used anyway, and that this property need not hold for biased noise models.
quotes: The quantum-enhanced algorithm should degrade gracefully with noise.
In the case of completely catastrophic depolarizing noise, the output of the quantum part is simply a uniformly random bit-string
This property need not hold for biased noise models.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper cites the result that generating samples from even constant-depth noiseless QAOA is hard for classical algorithms, given some reasonable computational complexity assumptions.
quotes: generating samples from even constant-depth noiseless QAOA is hard for classical algorithms [6] (given some reasonable computational complexity assumptions)
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper cites that state-of-the-art exact algorithms solve arbitrary instances of problems such as Max-Cut on up to about 100 variables, and that state-of-the-art heuristics solve instances on hundreds or thousands of variables to optimality in practice.
quotes: on up to about 100 variables [10], depending on the structure of the problem.
State-of-the-art heuristics can solve instances on hundreds or thousands of variables to optimality in practice [15].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in experiments on quantum hardware and in emulation, in some cases the quantum-enhanced running time is up to a factor of about 1000 lower than the original classical running time, measured by the Q-factor.
quotes: We find that, both in experiments on quantum hardware and in emulation, in some cases, the quantum-enhanced running time is up to a factor of ∼ 1000 lower than the original classical running time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The Q-factor counts iterations of the classical heuristic, not wall time, and excludes the time to obtain the samples (see the Q-factor definition and the runtime caveat).

assertions.value: The authors state that the running time improvement increases with problem size, up to instances on 40 qubits on quantum hardware.
quotes: In addition, the running time improvement increases with problem size, up to instances on 40 qubits on quantum hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim, not tested in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The hardware results in Sec. VII C show the line-graph Hamming-filter speedup overcome by noise at around 30 nodes and p = 4 outperforming p = 5 and p = 6 at N = 40, so the growth is not monotone in every setting.

assertions.value: The paper defines the Q-factor as the ratio of the minimal expected runtime of the heuristic with random initialization to that with warm starts, where the cost C(T) is the number of iterations T divided by the probability Fopt(T) of returning an optimal solution within T iterations. A value above 1 indicates a speedup.
quotes: C(T ) is the expected number of iterations required to find an optimal solution.
is to compute the ratio of the two minima obtained using different initialisation strategies:
where Q > 1 indicates a speedup, e.g. Q = 2 implies that the warm starts made the algorithm converge twice as quickly as the case where random bit-strings were used.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines it here.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the emulated experiments they track the number of iterations needed to reach the optimal cut, and use those statistics to estimate the expected runtime of the algorithm; the Q-factor is computed from iteration counts.
quotes: We keep track of the number of iterations required in each case to reach the optimal cut for the graph and used those statistics to estimate the expected runtime of the algorithm for a given set of initial strings.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup.

While it is possible to obtain better optimization results by e.g. performing the optimization more times or using more informed initial guesses, we wanted to demonstrate a bare-bones comparison

with N ∈ [20, 25] nodes and edge probabilities chosen between 0.1 and 0.9.

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proves that, for an alternating layered ansatz with blocks forming local 2-designs, global cost functions have exponentially vanishing gradient variance even at shallow depth while local cost functions have gradient variance bounded below polynomially at logarithmic depth, with a quantum autoencoder simulation up to 100 qubits.

existing.note: The result holds for a gradient-free optimizer whose number of shots per cost evaluation is capped (Methods, p.13). The paper says that in principle a minimizing direction can always be found for the global cost, at an exponentially growing shot count. For nB = 20 the global cost could be trained once the shot count rose. The ansatz is a real-coefficient simplification of the analysed one, and the input ensemble is one fixed two-state example with nA = 1.
existing.value: In simulations of a quantum autoencoder with two layers of the simplified ansatz, one non-trash qubit (nA = 1) and nB from 10 to 100 trash qubits, the authors report that they could train the global cost only up to nB = 20, while the local cost trained in all cases; the training used a gradient-free method with a cap on the number of shots per cost evaluation, and the ansatz does not satisfy the theorems exactly.

existing.note: The result is an upper bound on the variance of one partial derivative, for an operator O of the stated forms: case (i) a single product of non-trivial projectors with c1 squared times R growing at most as 2 to the n, or case (ii) any number N of terms (N at most of order 2 to the n) that are products of traceless operators with bounded Hilbert-Schmidt norm and constants of order one. Every block, and WA and WB, must form a local 2-design; the block size m does not grow with n, and the number of layers L is of order poly(log n). The exponential decay needs block size m of at least 2 (the text layer drops the sign).

papers.what_it_is: A review of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs): their structure (cost, ansatz, gradients, optimizers), applications, the challenges of trainability, efficiency and accuracy, and prospects for near-term quantum advantage.

existing.value: The review states that in a barren plateau the partial derivatives of the cost vanish on average exponentially with the system size, so exponentially large precision is needed to resolve a cost-minimizing direction for both gradient-based and gradient-free optimizers; it cites the original proof for deep randomly initialized unstructured circuits and states that noise can also induce barren plateaus regardless of the ansatz.

papers.title_in_file: Does provable absence of barren plateaus imply classical simulability?
papers.version_note: arXiv:2312.09121v3, 25 Aug 2025 (the file is named for 2023, the first version; the text is the 2025 v3 with the Supplemental Information on PDF pp.22-37). Matches the record; the record's quotes are checked against v3. The paper is a perspective that states two claims and gives case-by-case arguments; it reports no experiments ('No data was generated').
papers.what_it_is: A perspective article arguing, case by case, that many parametrized-circuit models with provably absent barren plateaus live in classically identifiable polynomial-size subspaces and so admit classical or quantum-enhanced classical simulation of the loss, with caveats and a contrived counterexample.

existing.note: The claim is limited to losses of the form in Eq. (1), to the barren plateau-free architectures the authors analysed (their Table 1), and to provable absence of barren plateaus. The authors call it evidence from a case-by-case study, not a proof; for models living in effective subspaces the simulation holds only with high probability over the parameters; and some models need no quantum data at all (the classical class CSIM). The paper says it does not claim that every non-concentrated loss is simulable.
existing.value: The authors collect evidence, case by case, that many commonly used models, those with provably barren plateau-free loss landscapes among the architectures they analysed, can also admit classical simulation of a loss of the stated expectation-value form, provided classical data are collected from quantum devices in an initial data acquisition phase for the cases that need it; they do not claim that every non-concentrated loss can be classically simulated.

quotes: We collect evidence—on a case-by-case basis—that many commonly used models whose loss landscapes avoid barren plateaus can also admit classical simulation, provided that one can collect some classical data from quantum devices during an initial data acquisition phase.
It was not possible to analyze every work claiming absence of barren plateaus—we studied only those in Table 1
We do not claim that BP ⊂ CpolySub. Thus we are not claiming that any non-concentrated loss can always be classically simulated.

B) that there is a problem class that is barren plateau-free but not in QESIM: a circuit consisting of a fixed polynomial-size circuit U implementing a Boolean function B(x) that is classically hard on random inputs even with advice strings, preceded by single-qubit X rotations with angles drawn from a discrete set so the input is a random computational basis state; B(x) has large variance over inputs, so the class is in BP, and as its hardness (not in BPP/poly, the many cryptographic discrete-logarithm problems being believed to satisfy this) rules out QESIM, BP is not contained in QESIM; the paper calls this example rather contrived.
quotes: In this section we showcase an example of a non-concentrated loss function which is not classically simulable. This example showcases that BP ≠ QESIM.

More specifically, we take U to be a quantum circuit that implements a Boolean function B(x) : {0, 1}n → {−1, 1} over the first output qubit that is classically hard to simulate for random input bitstrings, even with advice strings [77].
Equivalently, this can be stated as saying that this class of Boolean functions {B(x)} is not in BPP/poly.
